entries.title: compile the golden cases in one process instead of one each
entries.body:
* perf(tests): compile the golden cases in one process instead of one each

Section A of `tests/run.js` spawned `node dist/index.js` once per case in
`tests/cases/`, and almost none of that time was spent compiling. One
invocation costs 634 ms: 36 ms for Node to start, ~473 ms for
`import ts from "typescript"` in `src/parser.ts`, ~85 ms to load `dist/`, and
1.5 ms to compile the case. Paid once per case over six hundred cases, that is
an import bill rather than a test suite.

The cases are now compiled in process. `tests/batch_worker.js` drives
`new Compilation({})` / `addRoot` / `check` / `emit` directly, sixty-four cases
to a worker, and `tests/batch_compile.js` spawns the workers and hands
`tests/run.js` a result in the shape `spawnSync` answers in — so the section's
checks, its `PASS` / `FAIL` wording, its ordering and its skip accounting are
untouched. Two properties of the compiler are what make one process
shareable: a rejection comes back as a thrown `CompileError` rather than a
`process.exit`, and the IR is a pure function of the source, the options and
the *spelling* of the input path, which is handed over exactly as written
because `source_filename` and `-g`'s `DIFile` record it.

Nothing is quietly lost on the way. A `.args` flag the library API cannot
express — `--link`, `-o`, `--json`, the interop sidecars — is not ignored but
declined, and the case falls back to a real CLI spawn; so does every case when
`dist/` is missing. A worker that dies takes its chunk with it, so a dead chunk
is re-run one case per process and the case that dies on its own is reported as
a failure naming itself rather than falling through to a CLI run that would
pass.

The fast path is gated on the slow one rather than trusted. Every run compiles
one case per *shape* through the CLI as well — each distinct `.args` spelling in
the corpus, each sidecar a case asserts through, with and without a second
module — and compares the exit status, stdout, stderr and the bytes of the
emitted module. That set is derived from the corpus, so a case introducing a new
flag spelling joins the gate by existing. `node tests/run.js --verify-batch`
widens it to all of `tests/cases/`, which is what CI's new `batch-parity` job
runs on every pull request; a rotating sample was the alternative and was
rejected, because a gate that checks different cases on different days makes a
failure nobody can reproduce by re-running.

`llvm-as` and `opt -passes=verify` are left as two invocations wherever the
suite pairs them. They are two claims — that the textual IR assembles, and that
the module satisfies the verifier under the pass manager — and each is a `PASS`
line the summary counts, so collapsing them would trade about a hundred
assertions for a few seconds. What remains of section A's time is the native
link per `.out` case, which recompiles the C runtime every time; that is a
separate change.

Measured: section A 519 s -> 118 s over 623 cases on a 4-core Linux box; the compiles alone 395 s -> 5.3 s; the whole of `npm test` 24m21s -> 17m21s, `1652 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped` -> `1672 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped` (the 20 added passes are the gate)
Refs: .claude/testing.md
Tests: tests/run.js --verify-batch

* ci: name the batch-parity summary line instead of the line after it

`tests/run.js` prints the DEGRADED note *after* the `N passed` line when
anything skipped, so `tail -n 1` put the note in the job notice and left the
count out of it. Pick the line by what it says.

* test: format the batch files and key the gate set without a NUL byte

Two literal NUL bytes had ended up in the shape key, which made git treat
`tests/batch_compile.js` as a binary file and `grep` refuse to read it.
`JSON.stringify` of the triple says the same thing in printable text.

entries.title: link the golden cases against a runtime built once per run
entries.body:
Every case with a `.out` was linked by handing clang the module, the driver and
both runtime translation units, so `runtime/runtime.c`, `runtime/runtime_os.c`
and `tests/driver.c` were compiled again for each of the 183 of them. Measured
on a four-core Linux box, that link costs 470 ms; linking the same module
against prebuilt object files costs 91 ms, and building the objects costs
362 ms once.

`runtimeObjects(defines)` builds them on first use and `linkNative` is now the
one place a case is linked. The defines are the cache key and are the whole of
what can make one case need a differently built runtime: today that is
`-DNISH_THREADS=1` alone, which moves `nish_arena` into thread-local storage.

A wrong-but-fast link would be worse than the slow one it replaced, so the
cache is gated rather than trusted, by two checks at the end of the run — where
they can replay whatever the run actually linked:

- **The objects are what clang would have produced inline.** For each set of
  defines a case asked for, the first case linked with it is linked again from
  the sources, on the command line this suite used before the objects existed,
  argument for argument, and the two binaries have to be byte-identical.
- **The key is load-bearing.** A `--threads` module linked against the *default*
  objects has to **fail**: `ld` refuses a TLS reference against a non-TLS
  definition, so a case handed the wrong runtime is a link error rather than a
  program running with two arenas.

Nothing is cached across runs. The objects are built on their first use in each
process, so a `runtime.c` edited between runs cannot be linked against the
object a previous run left behind.

Three links still name the sources, on purpose, and say so beside the code: the
two runtime unit tests, whose subject *is* that the translation units compile
warning-free together, and the layout link, whose `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`
covers the runtime as well as `structs.c`. Caching those would take away a
check rather than an overhead. The `.text` budget measurements are untouched:
they compile with `-Oz -c` into their own object paths and share nothing with
the link cache.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: run an N-API export on libuv's thread pool with `--emit-napi-async`
entries.body:
* feat(interop): run an N-API export on libuv's thread pool with `--emit-napi-async`

`--emit-napi` writes a shim that calls the compiled function on whatever thread
N-API handed it, which for a `require()`d addon is Node's main thread, so a
function that runs for 200 ms blocks Node's event loop for 200 ms. That is the
defect [wp24-async.md](docs/wp24-async.md) §5.1 names as A1 and the one item
that note recommended building; WP20 T0's thread-local arena was its whole
prerequisite.

`--emit-napi-async <shim.c>` writes the same shim plus a promise-returning
`<name>Async` beside every export whose arguments and result are plain scalars:
`napi_create_async_work` runs the call on libuv's thread pool and
`napi_create_promise` / `napi_resolve_deferred` hand JavaScript a promise. The
compiled function does not change — it is exactly as synchronous as it was and
is still exported under its own name — so this adds **no language surface**, and
`docs/LANGUAGE.md` keeps every `async` / `await` / `yield` rejection it has.

Additive rather than replacing, because the synchronous export is what the WP8
batching benchmark calls and what a host wanting the answer *now* still wants: a
host chooses per call site instead of per build, and the two can be measured
against each other inside one addon. Without the flag the generated shim is
byte-identical, checked over the interop corpus.

`--threads` is required on both halves, and neither absence is silent. The
generated C opens with an `#error` unless `-DNISH_THREADS` is set, because one
process-wide bump allocator shared by two threads corrupts silently. The
compiler refuses `--emit-napi-async` without `--threads` as well, which is the
less obvious half: a module that allocates inline reads `@nish_arena` as a plain
global otherwise, and nothing downstream notices — contrary to what `nish.h`
says, a non-TLS reference links against the runtime's `_Thread_local` definition
without complaint in the `-shared -fPIC` napi profile. The exec callback
brackets the call with `nish_arena_mark` / `nish_arena_release` on the worker's
own arena, so a reused pool thread stays flat instead of growing for the life of
the process.

Scalars only, and the rest of the surface says why. A string or typed-array
parameter or result keeps its synchronous wrapper and is named in the shim with
the reason: the arena is per-thread, so a mark taken on the JS thread cannot be
released on the worker, and a typed array is *borrowed* from the JS
`ArrayBuffer`, which N-API guarantees only for the callback that read it. A
by-value `Result` parameter does cross, being scalars in a register read on the
JS thread; a `Result` result does not yet.

`<name>Async` rejects rather than throws, a bad argument included, because the
promise is created before the arguments are read — a promise-returning function
that threw synchronously would be the one failure a `.catch` cannot reach.

Measured: 218.06 ms of event-loop stall becomes 0.36 ms for a 220 ms call
Refs: docs/wp24-async.md, docs/wp8-interop.md
Tests: tests/self/interop_async.ts, examples/node-addon-async.mjs

* style(interop): an arrow bound to a const, and a const that is never reassigned

The two house rules in .claude/typescript.md, which the merge made visible:
`npm run lint` may not grow the warning backlog and this branch had taken it
from main's 683 to 685. `asyncWrapper` mirrored the `function` declaration of
the `wrapper` beside it instead of the arrow new code is supposed to be, and
stage1's `why` is never reassigned. Both are pure refactors: the generated
shim is byte-identical, and the only golden movement is the `(let)` that is
now `(const)`.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: skip the rolling freeze where no seed can exist, fail where one is missing
entries.body:
* ci(bootstrap): check the rolling freeze on both operating systems

WP19 G3 asks for the seeded build of `self/` on both operating systems and
has had it on one. Two things were in the way; this closes the mechanism and
measures what is left instead of estimating it.

`bootstrap` becomes a matrix over `ubuntu-latest` and `macos-latest`, and the
seed asset is named for the **host** -- `uname -s`/`uname -m` resolved to the
triple `release.yml` stamps into the tarball name, which is a contract between
the two workflows rather than a label. A release that carries no binary for
this host names the asset it wanted, warns that the rolling freeze is
unchecked there, and stops. It does not pass quietly: a freeze nobody checked
must not read as a freeze that held. The darwin row becomes a real check with
no further edit here on the day G5 ships the other three binaries.

The macOS `test` row is **not** restored, and the reason is no longer a guess.
It was run for the first time and `npm test` fails there with five failures in
four families, none of them a compiler bug and all of them checks that encode
an ELF/Linux assumption:

  - `llvm-dwarfdump` reports an empty `.debug_line` for the linked binary,
    twice. On Mach-O `clang -g` leaves DWARF in the `.o` files and the
    executable carries only a debug map; `dsymutil` is what produces a line
    table.
  - `--threads` IR **links** against a runtime built without
    `-DNISH_THREADS` and exits 0. ELF refuses a TLS symbol against a non-TLS
    definition; ld64 does not. The safety net `build.sh`'s header describes
    does not exist on macOS, which is a finding about the platform rather
    than about the check.
  - `stage3 == stage2` as files fails at *identical size*, 597,048 bytes
    both. Every IR equality passes, so the compiler is deterministic and the
    linker is not: Mach-O's debug map records each `.o`'s path and mtime.

The last of those reaches past this job: `scripts/bootstrap.sh --verify`
asserts the same comparison, so it stands between the release workflow and a
darwin binary too (G5). Porting four checks against hardware that has to be
iterated on is a package of its own, and the bash 3.2 defects that used to
block the row are genuinely fixed -- these are what was behind them.

Refs: docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md#g3-the-seed-protocol-exists-and-ci-uses-it
Refs: docs/wp10-ci.md#ci-matrix

* ci(bootstrap): fail when there is no seed, and say what macOS still needs

The `bootstrap` job is the only thing that checks WP19's rolling freeze, and
it had a branch that reported success having checked nothing: with no seed for
its host it named the asset it wanted, printed a `::warning::` and exited 0.
A warning above a green check is a green check, and `CLAUDE.md` reads a green
check as permission to merge. That is the shape §A5 of
`docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md` is the written record of — a gate wearing the
colour of a gate that held — so the branch is gone. No release, or a release
carrying nothing for this host, is now a **red job** with the asset named in
the annotation.

Three smaller things follow from the same step:

- The seed lookup runs **before** the LLVM install and `npm ci`. It needs `gh`
  and the checkout and nothing else, so a host with no seed answers in seconds
  instead of paying for a toolchain it is about to throw away.
- Its outputs reach bash through `env:` rather than through `${{ }}` spliced
  into the script — the rule `pr-title.yml` already states for a step holding
  text it did not write.
- `release.yml` named `macos-latest` being out of the CI matrix as what darwin
  waits on. A release asset is built on a tag, so the test matrix would not
  supply one either way. It now names the four triple spellings `ci.yml`
  resolves to, because those are the contract between the two workflows, and
  the `--verify` comparison ld64 fails.

**The macOS `bootstrap` row goes with the macOS `test` row, and for a reason
the same run measured.** The fourth of the five darwin failures is
`stage3 == stage2` at identical size, and that is the comparison
`scripts/bootstrap.sh --verify` makes — so a seeded macOS row would be red on
the day G5 shipped its seed, not a check that had been waiting to pass. The
darwin half of G3 is short two things rather than one, and the documents say
so instead of saying the runner half is closed. The seed lookup is written for
any host already, so the row costs `ci.yml` a matrix over the two runners once
both have landed.

Refs: docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md#g3-the-seed-protocol-exists-and-ci-uses-it
Refs: docs/wp10-ci.md#ci-matrix

* fix(docs): slug heading anchors the way GitHub does, not the way that passes

`docs/check-links.mjs` is the gate that keeps the guidelines' graph of pointers
honest, and it disagreed with GitHub about what a heading's anchor is. GitHub
slugs with `github-slugger`, which is three steps: lower-case, **delete** every
character that is not a letter, a number, a mark, `_` or `-`, then turn each
remaining space into one `-`. The checker collapsed whitespace runs instead
(`.replace(/\s+/g, "-")`), which is the same answer for a heading whose words
are separated by single spaces and a different one for every heading holding an
em dash, a slash or any other deleted character with a space on each side:
`G5 — Distribution does not need Node` is `g5--distribution-does-not-need-node`
on github.com and was `g5-distribution-…` here. It also dropped `_`, which
GitHub keeps.

So the gate passed while the links landed nowhere — the documentation version
of the defect the rest of this branch is about, and the reason the fix is in
the slug function rather than in the four call sites that happened to show it.

Measured against GitHub itself: the rendered HTML of eight documents
(`/repos/amritk/nish/contents/<path>` with `Accept: application/vnd.github.html`)
carries 292 heading ids. The old rule got 49 of them wrong and the new rule
gets none. The new character class also agrees with `github-slugger` 2.0.0 on
all 886 headings in this repository; it is not that package's 8 KB generated
table, which deletes code points that were unassigned when it was generated and
are letters now, in scripts nothing here is written in.

Five anchors were then landing nowhere, and are corrected: the four this branch
added to em-dash headings in `wp10-ci.md` and `wp19-stage0-retirement.md`, and
one that has been broken on `main` — `LANGUAGE.md`'s link to
`wp6-memory.md#4-t-null`, whose heading is `## 4. \`T | null\`` and whose anchor
is `#4-t--null`. Those five now fail under the old rule and pass under the new
one, which is the fix pinning itself: a regression to whitespace-collapsing
turns the link gate red rather than quiet.

Refs: docs/check-links.mjs
Tests: node docs/check-links.mjs — 523 links in 40 Markdown files, ok; the same
  tree under the previous slug rule reports 7 broken anchors, all of them
  spellings github.com resolves

* ci(bootstrap): make the seeds a release attaches the matrix, and check the lookup

The job that checks WP19's rolling freeze has now been wrong in both
directions, a round apart, and the reason is that it had three answers and two
colours.

It first named the asset it wanted, warned, and exited 0 — and a warning above
a green check is a green check, which is exactly the shape
`docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md` §A5 is the written record of. The correction
for that made every seed it could not find **red**, which is the opposite
error and reaches further: `release.yml`'s `release` job is `needs: ci`, so a
repository with no release — the 0.1.0 base case `docs/wp12-release.md`
documents, and every fork on the day it is forked — could never cut the
release that would supply the seed the gate was waiting for. That is the same
argument this branch uses to keep the macOS `test` row out, applied to a job
sitting on the release path.

The three states are genuinely different, so the workflow stops conflating
them. `seeds` asks the last release which seed binaries it attaches, and
`bootstrap` is a **matrix over that answer** — one row per seed that actually
exists:

| The checks list says | It means |
| --- | --- |
| `seeds` green, a `bootstrap (<seed>)` row green | the freeze was checked with that seed, on that seed's own platform, and it held |
| `seeds` green, no row for a platform | the freeze was *not* checked there, and nothing is wrong: no release carries a seed for it yet. The `seeds` summary names every platform in both states |
| `seeds` green, `bootstrap` **skipped** | the same for every platform at once: there is no release at all |
| `seeds` **red** | a seed that should exist does not — a release missing an asset `release.yml` attaches |
| a `bootstrap` row **red** | `self/` does not build with the last release: the rolling freeze broken, which is what the pair exists to catch |

Which missing seed is red is decided by platform, and the decision is data:
`.github/seed-targets.json` marks a platform `attached` when `release.yml`
builds a seed for it. A release that attaches no
`nish-<version>-x86_64-linux.tar.gz` is a regression in that workflow or in
the asset name the two share, and it costs the freeze its only check, so it is
red — with the recovery in the annotation, because that red blocks the release
that would fix it. Darwin is not that: nothing builds the binary yet (G5), so
there is no row and the `seeds` summary says the freeze is unchecked there.
A platform's row appears the day a release carries its seed, with no edit to
`ci.yml`, because the matrix is the release's answer rather than a list in the
workflow.

**The lookup is a file now, and `npm test` runs it.** Both times this logic was
got wrong it was inline shell in a workflow that nothing could run, and the
second time was one round after the first. `.github/seed-matrix.sh` is the step
body, and the new WP19 block of `tests/run.js` drives it against a stand-in for
`gh` through each state: the seed present, the `attached` seed missing (exit 1
with the `::error::`), a seed missing for a platform nothing builds one for, no
release at all, and a seed appearing for a platform that had none — which is
the claim that the macOS row arrives with no edit here, checked rather than
asserted in a comment.

The script reads that file with `jq`, which the runner images ship and a
workstation may not, so the five runs that drive it skip rather than fail
without it — the rule the rest of the suite follows for a tool it cannot
install, and a third permitted environmental skip in `AGENTS.md`. The checks
that compare the file against the compiler's target table are Node's own and
always run.

**The four asset spellings are one file rather than two comments calling each
other a contract.** `release.yml` hard-coded `nish-$version-x86_64-linux` while
a comment beside it listed four names as the triples `ci.yml` resolves to, and
two of those four were fiction: the compiler has never accepted
`aarch64-darwin` or `x86_64-darwin` — it knows `aarch64-apple-darwin`,
`x86_64-apple-darwin` and their aliases. `.github/seed-targets.json` carries
the canonical triple and the derived asset name for each platform, both
workflows read it, and `tests/run.js` checks every row against
`src/codegen/target.ts`: the triple is one the compiler calls canonical, and
the asset is that triple with the vendor and the ABI dropped.

`scripts/bootstrap.sh` also gains the note it was missing. The `stage3 ==
stage2` comparison was cited from a workflow comment by line number — a
reference that rots on the next edit — while the comparison itself said nothing
about Mach-O, where two links of identical input differ. That is measured
rather than expected, and it stands in front of both a darwin seed and a darwin
release binary, so whoever next touches that line now meets the finding at the
line.

Nothing here adds the macOS row: until G5 ships a darwin seed it is the second
state above, and the ld64 fixed point would make it red the day the seed
arrived.

Refs: docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md#g3--the-seed-protocol-exists-and-ci-uses-it, docs/wp10-ci.md#the-seeded-build-and-what-a-missing-seed-reports
Tests: tests/run.js "WP19: the seed-target contract" — 9 checks, five of them
  driving .github/seed-matrix.sh against a stubbed `gh`, one per state; both
  workflows parse as YAML and every `run:` step under `bash -n`

* docs(cli): say five, which is how many anchors the corrected slug rule caught

The comment beside the slug fix said four -- the anchors this branch added --
and the run that followed it found a fifth, standing on `main`:
`LANGUAGE.md`'s link to `wp6-memory.md#4-t-null`, whose heading is
`## 4. \`T | null\`` and whose anchor is `#4-t--null`.

Refs: docs/check-links.mjs

* docs(cli): name all five states the seed-matrix checks cover

The list in wp10-ci.md skipped the one this round is about: a release that
attaches no seed for a platform nothing builds one for, which is expected and
green, as against the `attached` one that is missing, which is red.

Refs: docs/wp10-ci.md#the-seeded-build-and-what-a-missing-seed-reports

entries.title: close contiguous class arrays by costing the migration
entries.body:
WP15 §2a shipped contiguous storage for `interface` elements and left class
elements out, calling the migration "the work, not the layout"; §9 item 7 called
it "its own item". The migration has now been costed against the program that
would have to survive it, and it is not a migration of `self/`: it changes what
`T[]` means for every class `T`, and `self/` is only the largest program caught
by it. So an array of classes is one pointer per slot **by decision**, and item
7 is closed rather than deferred.

Three findings, each counted by walking every file in `self/` with the
TypeScript compiler API rather than by grep, because the obvious grep is what
got the first draft of this wrong.

**One `FunctionSig`, three holders.** `collectMethod` pushes the same signature
into `owner.methodSigs` and into `ctx.program.functions`, and `collectConstructor`
does the same with `owner.ctor`. Pass 2 reaches it through `program.functions`
and writes `sig.poisoned = true`; the emitter reaches it through `methodSigs`.
With value slots those are two copies and a pointer, so the emitter emits a body
the checker rejected. `declareStruct` has the same shape one level up. A stage1
built with class arrays as values rejects `self/` with 41 errors of the form
"Field ctor of class StructInfo has no initializer and no constructor assigns
it".

**54 identity comparisons.** Under the rule "a `===` or `!==` whose two operands
are both class-typed, where at least one is an element read out of a class-typed
array, either `a[i]` or the binding of a `for (const x of a)`": 54 operators on
50 lines in 10 modules — `bounds.ts` 20, `attributes.ts` 13, `escape.ts` 11,
`checker.ts` 4, and one each in six more. Widened to every class-typed identity
comparison in `self/`, element-sourced or not, it is 80 across 19 modules.

**In `self/bounds.ts` the failure mode is a miscompile, not a slow program.**
Twenty of the 54 are there and they split in two. The *lookups* answering "not
found" only lose proofs, and a check that survives is indeed a slower program.
The *invalidation* is the other half — `forget` and `forgetUpperBounds`, which
the module's own header calls "the whole soundness argument" — nine operators on
seven lines, each keeping a fact by testing `!==` against the variable being
clobbered. An identity test that never matches makes those guards always true,
so no fact is retracted: a one-element array indexed after an increment compiles
to no bounds check at all and exits 0 where it should panic.

The suite already says so, so nothing new had to be written. The invalidation
half is caught by `perf_bounds_loop`, whose first case loses its `bounds.fail`
block; the lookup half is caught by `arr_bounds_proven` and `perf_bounds_quiet`,
goldens whose assertion is the *absence* of a check. A regression that would be
`self/`'s alone is caught by `tests/self/ir_oracle.js`.

**And the syntax tree would become storage.** `Node.children` is a `Node[]`, so
value elements copy every node once per level of nesting, and
`list.children[i] === node` stops being answerable at all. `Local` and `Node`
lead the 168 class-typed array slot declarations in `self/`, at 47 and 18.

What the layout buys is available today by declaring the element type an
`interface`, and `C | null` is the way back to a pointer array; what a class
element would add over that is methods and a constructor on the element type,
against changing what `xs.push(c); c.m()` means in a language where nothing else
copies a class.

Source changes are the JSDoc on `inlineElementStruct` in each compiler, which
said "a separate change with a migration of its own" and now says the decision.
No behaviour change and no IR change; the stage1 checked dump is re-recorded
because `--emit-checked` prints a line:column per local and callee.
metrics: 54 identity comparisons on 50 lines in 10 modules (20 in `self/bounds.ts`, 9 of them in the invalidation guards); 80 class-typed identity comparisons in all, across 19 modules; 168 class-typed array slot declarations over 36 element classes (`Local` 47, `Node` 18); a stage1 built with value elements rejects `self/` with 41 errors
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: refute the invariant array header and re-scope item 1b
entries.body:
WP15 §9 item 1b proposed marking an array's header loads `!invariant.load` so
the length and data pointer could be hoisted out of a loop. Candidate 1 — the
`readonly T[]` spelling of it — is refuted, and the item is re-scoped to
candidate 2 rather than closed.

**Candidate 1 is a miscompile, not an optimisation declined.** `!invariant.load`
is scoped to the program and the dereferenceable window, not to a function or a
call, so a caller that pushes between two reads is undefined. The twenty-line
counter-example prints `6 10` unmarked and `6 6` with every header load in the
module marked — the five of them, including the three in `@nish_main` where the
`push` is. Marking only the two inside the callee, which is the whole of what a
`readonly` parameter could justify, still prints `6 10`: the worse position
rather than a sound one, an entitlement LLVM has not cashed. Applied across
`self/` it is 7,068 header loads over 60 modules, and the marked build is a
22,048-byte compiler — 2.2% of the 988,296-byte unmarked one — that answers
``compile: unknown flag `tiny.ts` `` because `self/options.ts` is where argv
parsing lives. The deletion is what reproduces; its severity is not, and two
earlier heads on one box did not link at all where a second box linked at three
different mark counts, all at clang/LLD 18.1.3.

**The field shape is where the remaining win is, and `self/` is written that
way.** Everything §2b banked was measured on a loop over two array parameters.
An array reached through a class field — `while (i < h.xs.length) dst[i] =
h.xs[i] * 2.0` — runs at 756 ms against the parameter shape's 305, and a
source-level `const xs = h.xs` recovers all of it. `self/bounds.ts`'s
`knownAtMost` is that shape verbatim, and 24 functions in that one module carry
a header load inside a loop, so the earlier claim that nothing in `bench/` or
`self/` reproduces it was false.

**The mechanism is vectorisation, and it sharpens the acceptance criterion.** No
field-shape build has a header load in its hot loop — once the callee inlines
they are all hoisted, in every variant — so "the header is re-read every
iteration" never explained the 2.48x. What separates the builds is that the
parameter shape's two lengths become one trip count (`llvm.umin.i64` in the
preheader) and its loop has one exit, while the field shape reads the length
twice, for the loop condition and for the bounds check, keeps two exits, and the
vectoriser declines: 0 packed instructions against 4. So "hoist the header once
per loop" is satisfiable while buying nothing — a preheader load plus a fresh
length per bounds check satisfies it and still runs at ~750 ms, which a probe
that removes every header load from the loop by hand confirms at 761 ms. The
criterion is **one length value feeding both the loop condition and the bounds
check**, and the thing to look for is the `umin`, or one compare where there
were two.

Item 1b is therefore open for candidate 2 — hoisting in the emitter — with the
field-shape program as its acceptance program, 2.48x as its acceptance number,
and the whole-program "does not grow an array" fact `attributes.ts` lacks as its
prerequisite. §2c also names the one other live proposal the same refutation
kills: `wp9-optimisation.md` proposes marking array *data* loads `!invariant.load`
"inside that function" for a function that never stores an element, and there is
no "inside that function" for a program-scoped marking — over an arena that
never frees, the dereferenceable window is the whole process.

A guard in `tests/run.js` pins that the alias-domain win §2b banked is still
there, described as what it is: the parameter shape only.
metrics: field shape 756 ms against 305 for the parameter shape, both recovered to 305 by a source hoist; 0 packed instructions against 4; 761 ms with every header load removed from the loop by hand; 7,068 marks over 60 modules linking a 22,048-byte compiler against 988,296 unmarked
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: monomorphise generic classes and interfaces
entries.body:
`class Box<T>` and `interface Pair<A, B>` compile, and an instantiation is an
ordinary struct. `Box<i32>` is `%struct.Box$i32` with `Box`'s fields at
`T = i32`; its members are `@Box$i32.constructor` and `@Box$i32.get`, and the
layout computation, `implements`, `new`, field access, the C header, the DWARF
composite type and the escape analysis all work on it unchanged. Nothing was
added to `StaticType`, and a type parameter is still never a type: a template's
annotations stay as syntax, and one instantiation resolves them with `T` bound.

Type arguments are written out in the two positions a one-token parser can read
a list in — an annotation, and after `new`. A call still infers, and a field may
not grow its own type argument.

Two defects were found on the way and are fixed here. `containsType` walked
arrays, nullables and `Result` payloads but not an instantiated struct's type
arguments, so `grow<T>` asking for `grow<Box<T>>` did not terminate; it reads
them back out of the instantiation set now, which closes the same hole on the
function side. And two modules that each declared `Holder<T>` and instantiated
it at `i32` both produced `%struct.Holder$i32`: the second registration replaced
the layout the first module's objects were built with, so a field read landed on
the wrong offset — 118 instead of 229, with no diagnostic — and `llvm-as` then
refused the entry module. Packages make `Holder` and `Holder` two names; they
make no difference at all to `Holder$i32`, which is a program-wide struct name
and a program-wide method symbol whoever asked for it. The check runs after
`drainInstantiations`, where the instantiation set is final, and covers the
same-package case that is every ordinary two-module program.

A struct needed a C spelling of its own: `--emit-header` wrote `struct Box$i32`
and `-pedantic` refuses `$` in an identifier. A declared class passes through
untouched, so every existing program's header says what it always said; an
instantiation is `nish_gen_` — reserved, because `nish_` is already refused in a
declared name — followed by the collapse with the user's own `_` escaped, which
is what keeps `Box_arr<i32>` and `Box<i32[]>` apart.

Termination is a request chain on the struct side too, so there is still no
template graph and a diagnostic names the concrete chain. `implements` is
checked per instantiation rather than at the template, which costs a repeated
message and buys an interface that may itself be an instantiation.

Size, measured at `--profile size`: one copy of the body per distinct
type-argument tuple and nothing else. The one-instantiation row is 732 B of
`.text` in a 5,192 B binary — the same to the byte as the generic-function row.

Left for later and named in the note: G7's symbol prefix (an instantiated
class's methods are minted with the instantiating module's prefix, correct only
because importing a template is refused), G8's display name, and
`cFunctionName`'s collision.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: let the checker state the member-header rules the parser was eating
entries.body:
Four class-member-header wordings move from stage1's parser to its checker:
`x?: T`, `x!: T`, `m?()` and `static`. stage1's parser turned each of them down
where it stood, so the user saw a syntax error where stage0 named the member.
That is usually the right habit — lex and parse what is written, refuse in the
phase that owns the rule — and here it was the wrong phase, because all four
sentences name the member, say whether it is a field or a method, and name the
class it is in, and the parser knows none of those three things. It records
now, and `collectField`, `collectMethod` and `collectConstructor` state the
rules in stage0's words at stage0's spans.

The orders are deliberately different on the two members, because stage0's are:
a field's marker is read before its modifiers and a method's modifiers before
its marker, so `static x?: i32` and `readonly m?()` each get one sentence from
both compilers. Because stage0 reports the first modifier a member cannot carry
in source order, the parser also records which of `static`/`readonly` came
first.

Moving a rule out of the parser made three defects reachable that the parser
had been hiding, and all three are fixed here. A `static constructor()`
compiled, linked and ran on stage1 — exit 41, the body executed as the
*instance* constructor — because `parseMember` built the constructor node and
dropped the modifiers it had just read. A member *named* `static` produced four
syntax errors where stage0 names an optional field called `static`. And
`readonly` on a method was a rule stage1 did not have at all, so
`readonly m(): i32 {}` and `readonly constructor()` compiled where stage0
refuses them.

An interface field takes the modifiers too, which was one call: `interface I {
readonly x: i32 }` compiles on stage1 as on stage0, and `interface I { static
x: i32 }` names the field. It does not take `!` — a property signature cannot
carry one, so there is no stage0 sentence to agree with and the syntax error
stays right.

Neither gate could see the constructor bug, and that is the part worth keeping.
The constructor's sentence shares NL2116 with the method's, so
`diagnostic_coverage.js` counted the code covered by the method case and could
not see that the constructor sentence was unreached; and the corpus had no
program of that shape. The same trap turned up a second time in this branch on
NL2027, whose *interface* sentence shared a code with its class one: with the
new case removed, `--strict-refusals` still exits 0 and the coverage figure does
not move. Both now have a case that reaches the sentence itself.

Three oracle bails go with them. `tests/parser_oracle.js` skipped every
`PropertyDeclaration` with a `questionToken`, every member with
`StaticKeyword`, and every interface member with a `questionToken`, so those
shapes were parsed by stage1 with nothing comparing the tree against the
`typescript` parser's.

What the move costs is decided rather than discovered: a rule the checker owns
is a rule the member has to *parse* to reach, so eight shapes that used to hear
`static members are not supported` from the parser now hear the syntax error
about their other defect. Both compilers still refuse every one of them; the
difference is a declared one that `--parity` and `reject_oracle.js` count, and
the shapes are named in `parseMemberModifiers`, in the R3 row and in four cases.

Measured: parser oracle 767 -> 781 files compared (97 skipped), reject oracle
339 -> 353 cases with the parser bucket 92 -> 89, parser_refusals.txt 45 -> 41
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: add the codemod and the byte-for-byte IR diff stage C's rewrite needs
entries.body:
WP22 stage C's expensive half is 733 `function` declarations in `self/`, and
the only check that all of them are meaning-preserving is the bootstrap
comparing stage1's output against itself — the slowest check in the repository,
and one that runs after the rewrite is already in the tree. This adds the two
tools that make "did this rewrite change anything?" a single command, and runs
the §8a hunt before the rewrite rather than during it.

`arrowify.mjs` rewrites a `function` declaration to a `const` bound to an
arrow. It is textual but driven by the parse tree: every splice position — the
keyword, the parentheses, the return type — is a token read off the
declaration, because a comment is allowed to contain any of them.
`arrow-verify.mjs` copies the tracked tree, compiles every subject in scope,
changes the copy in place, compiles again, and hands each subject to one
`verdict`, which answers with exactly one of: absent on one side, refused on
one side only, refused on both for different words, refused on both for the
same words, compiled and emitted, compiled and dumped, or nothing to compare —
and the last fails the run, because a subject with nothing to compare is not
evidence.

**The hunt found no compiler bug.** §8a's shape is a pass that decides what a
value is *for* by climbing to its parent and expecting a statement. Every
parent-consulting pass divides into three kinds, and the middle one is the kind
to remember: `classifyUse` and `classifyElementUse` are right about arrows not
by design but by fallthrough, because an unrecognised parent is the
conservative answer. An arm added for `ts.isReturnStatement` and not for the
arrow puts them straight back in the class. One gap exists, is unreachable and
is identical in both compilers: `capturesLocal` and `isLocalRef` treat a
`return` as a capture and have no arm for the expression an arrow is, but the
scan they belong to looks for captures before an assignment in the same body,
and a concise body has no statement for an assignment to be in.

What the review rounds found instead were defects in this tooling, and one of
them kept coming back in different clothes: the sweep reporting success over
ground it never checked. A rewrite that had already been applied compiled the
same source twice and answered zero. A `reject_*` case that started *compiling*
was printed as a position shift. A whole-tree rewrite was reported beside a
slice-scoped comparison. A file emitted only after the rewrite was invisible. A
refusal with no diagnostics compared one empty string with another. A subject
that did not exist before the change crashed the run. And a successful
compile's diagnostics were read on neither side — which matters because this
tool's own argument is that a diagnostic carries a line and a column, the
parity gate is keyed on them, and a declaration that changes shape can move one
without moving a byte of IR. 51 of `self/`'s modules warn on a clean compile,
and §8b's recipe collapses bodies with `--concise`, which changes line numbers
by construction.

So the decision lives in one place now, and each of those is a row in
`npm test` rather than a sweep nobody re-runs. Every fix ships with the case
that reproduces it, and each was checked by reverting it.

Two properties change the migration plan. `useConsistentArrowReturn` is a Biome
*error*, so a block-only rewrite of `self/` would land 119 lint failures, one
per single-return declaration — the rewrite is therefore two passes, and
collapse goes second so a difference has one cause. And a block-bodied rewrite
moves no line, but it moves the function's own name three columns left and,
where a body shares a line with its declaration, everything inside it three
columns right. `self/` has no single-line body; the corpus has 77, 76 of them
`reject_*` cases where a column is what the diagnostic carries, and no gate
sees the shift because the `.err` sidecars pin words and both compilers move
together.

`tests/cases/fn_arrow_hoisting` pins the property everything rests on and that
nothing had asked: a module-level `const` bound to an arrow is a function
declaration, so it is in scope for the whole module and not only below its own
line. That is the difference between stage C being a spelling change and stage
C being a reordering of a compiler. `fn_arrow_concise_flow` is the positive
half of the hunt, a concise body in each position the other passes decide.

**Nothing here migrates `self/` and nothing enables stage D.** Enabling the
rejection turns every remaining `function` in the corpus into an error, so it
belongs with the migration.

Measured: the self/ sweep rewrites 733 declarations across 55 of 64 files, with
1396 emitted files and 51 warning surfaces compared and 0 differences; arrow 66
and package 56 from a clean build/test
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: resolve a package by name through the `nish` export condition
entries.body:
A bare import specifier now resolves through `node_modules` and the `nish`
export condition, and what it resolves to is the package's *source*:

    import { scale } from "pkg_bare";        // exports -> "."
    import { twice } from "pkg_bare/util";   // exports -> "./util"
    import { seed } from "@scope/hash";      // a scoped name

A package says it is Nish by declaring the condition, and its value is the file
an Nish consumer compiles. The number mode rides in the condition — `nish-i32`
and `nish-f64` are the mode-qualified spellings — and the compiler asks for its
own mode before it asks for plain `nish`. That rank is the compiler's, not the
manifest's, which is the one place this reader departs from Node: matching both
in one declaration-order walk meant a manifest declaring `nish` above `nish-f64`
compiled the mode-agnostic file under `--number-mode f64`, so the source the
package wrote for that mode was unreachable and nothing said so. `nish-f64` is
not a rival of `nish` but `nish` refined by the mode, and the refinement is not
the package's to rank. A package that offers this compiler no file fails saying
so rather than with a module-not-found that reads like the consumer's own typo.

Both manifest readers are the same narrow scan rather than a `JSON.parse` on one
side and a hand-rolled reader on the other, because the two compilers have to
select the same file for the same manifest — a program that resolved under one
and not the other is a program that compiles with one compiler and not the
other. What the narrowing costs is written in both module headers rather than
left to be discovered, and `tests/self/support_oracle.js` drives both over 51
cases where they agree line for line.

The walk is where the two compilers actually did differ, twice. stage1's climb
ran out where `dirname` does, so an ordinary `proj/node_modules` beside
`proj/src/main.ts` resolved under stage0 and failed under stage1. And Node steps
over a directory already called `node_modules` rather than searching it, which
stage0 could apply the whole way up because an absolute path names every
ancestor and stage1 could not. Naming a directory from below takes `getcwd` or
an inode to compare, and the language has neither by two separate decisions — so
rather than declare the divergence, `findPackageDir` now walks the importing
module's *name*, the one string both compilers hold, and the two visit the same
directories in the same order because they are given the same input and take the
same steps. A 256-level limit ends a spelled walk that cannot recognise the
filesystem root.

A symlinked package is a second package here, and that is declared rather than
fixed: the language has no `realpath`, and a stage0 that resolved symlinks would
compile programs stage1 refuses — trading a limitation the two compilers share
for a divergence between them.

Two seams found by review and closed here. `noNishEntryPoint`'s second clause
could be false — with the mode-qualified condition outranking the plain one, a
manifest whose `nish-i32` names a non-file never reaches its perfectly good
`nish` row — so it reports what the compiler came away with instead of what the
manifest declares. And the module a manifest names was accepted by a file test
and then read unguarded, so an unreadable one gave a span-less absolute-path
sentence where stage1 words the failure itself; the read moves into the import
loop and takes stage1's own two-way branch.

**A runtime contract narrowed.** `nish_read_file_or_null` had no guard at all:
`open(O_RDONLY)` accepts a directory, `lseek` then answers `LONG_MAX`, and the
arena was asked for that many bytes — so a package whose `exports` named a
directory, which this stage made reachable, died `nish: out of memory` on stage1
where stage0 gave a clean spanned diagnostic, and a `package.json` that was
itself a directory diverged on the exit code. The guard is `!S_ISDIR` on an
`fstat` of the descriptor: a directory is the only thing whose `lseek(SEEK_END)`
answers `LONG_MAX`, so `/dev/null` still reads as `""` on both sides, where an
`S_ISREG` test would have closed one divergence and opened a narrower one.
`readFileSyncOrNull` therefore answers `null` for a path that cannot be read as
a file — missing, a directory, a parent that cannot be searched, a pipe with no
length to ask for — and `docs/LANGUAGE.md` and the shipped `runtime/nish.d.ts`
both say so.

An earlier commit body on this branch claims an unguarded `readFileSync` was
reported as exit 70. It never could be: `isSystemError` catches every
`ErrnoException` and answers exit 1. What was wrong was the wording, and this is
the account to keep.

Measured: reject oracle 356/356 over 366 fragments, package 92/0, self 126/0/1
with IR(stage0) == IR(stage1) == IR(stage2) and stage3 == stage2 over 406
programs; runtime_os.c 1,251 bytes against a 1,280 budget, unchanged by the
guard
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: add `CPtr`, the opaque pointer a C function hands back
entries.body:
A C function that returns a handle — a `FILE *`, an allocation, a library
context — now has a type to return it as. `CPtr` is opaque by construction: a
program can hold one, compare two for identity, pass one back to a foreign
function, and nothing else. It has no arithmetic, no indexing, no field access,
no printing and no template interpolation, and each of those refusals names the
position it was written in.

The point of the opacity is that the compiler knows nothing about what the
pointer addresses, so it must not be allowed anywhere its ignorance would
matter. A `CPtr` cannot be a field, an array element, a `Result` payload, a
type argument, or a module constant, and it cannot cross `--emit-dts`. Those
are one rule with six position sentences rather than six rules, which is why
they share a code.

The refusals hold in both compilers at the same span, and the escape analysis
needs no change to be safe: `isPointerParam` and the escape classifier are both
allow-lists over the types the compiler owns, so a foreign pointer falls out of
each by construction rather than by an omission. No `nocapture`, `noalias`,
`dereferenceable` or `align` lands on a foreign `i8*`, and `CPtr === CPtr`
lowers to `icmp eq i8*`. The arena is untouched; no compiler-allocated pointer
crosses the boundary in either direction.

Two seams found by review and closed here. The array-element refusal spanned
the whole annotation on stage0 and the element on stage1, a divergence in a
rule this change introduces: `T[]` was the only spelling reporting on the
annotation, while `Array<T>`, `ReadonlyArray<T>` and both `Result` arms already
reported on the argument, and the message names the element, so the element is
what it underlines. `readonly CPtr[]` had the same split through the type
operator and takes the same fix. And the type-argument rule was implemented in
both compilers and reached by no test — the case named for it is caught by the
field rule first — so a generic function now reaches it, verified by deleting
the rule from each compiler in turn and watching that case, and only that case,
fail.

One shape escapes the type-argument rule and is recorded rather than closed: a
generic class with no member of its parameter's type, `class Empty<T> { n: i32
= 0; }` at `Empty<CPtr>`, reaches no member rule and `instantiateStruct` has no
check of its own. Nothing unsound follows — the instantiation lays out one
`i32` and no pointer is stored or exported — but the rule as stated is wider
than the rule as enforced, and both compilers carry a `TODO` saying so.

Measured: npm test 1858 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped, undegraded; ffi_pointer
24/0, reject 451/0, reject oracle 365/365 over 377 fragments
